1:
Who the destroyer is, and whom the four short orders address, gets more answers than the passage has clauses. Calvin sets out three constructions. On the first the verb means vanished rather than ascended, so the waster has disappeared before the chosen people and the orders are comfort: let every man go back to his city and keep watch, look out which way the invader came and find it clear, gird the loins and stand firm, the monarchy that oppressed them being now to be cut off. On the second they are a terror spoken during a siege, bidding the besieged guard their fortresses and warning that it will avail nothing. On the third the address is to the Assyrians and the destroyer is the Babylonian, a people surrounded with provinces and fortified cities being told its expectation will fail.

The rest take that last course and differ only over the man. Gill rejects the reading that makes this the Assyrian coming against Jerusalem, ascribing it to one Jewish commentator, and follows another in making it the Babylonian, not the famous king of that name but his father, who joined the Mede in taking the city. Clarke names the same pair and calls the chapter a set-piece of Hebrew poetry, giving the muster of the armies, the siege, the flooding of the river and the sack. Henry makes the destroyer the Babylonian and reports that the word may equally be rendered scatter; Wesley says only that they are Medes or Chaldeans.

That the four orders are ironical is agreed by two. Ellicott calls them sententious and of course ironical, comparing the directions given to the priests of the false god on the mountain, and thinks the man who dashes in pieces may be the Median king. Henry writes the irony out: secure the towers and magazines, set guards on the avenues, encourage the soldiers, fortify as cities do when an enemy advances, and still the stroke will not be put by, since there is no counsel or strength against the Lord.

The second verse divides them on a single verb. Gill and Calvin read it of a turning away. Gill takes it as a reckoning for the insolence of two Assyrian kings against the two kingdoms, the rod of God's anger now smarting in its turn. Calvin argues it out: some render that God makes the ancient glory of his people return, taking the noun in a good sense, and find a promise of restoration here; but the noun is far more often used in a bad sense, of haughtiness, and he prefers the sense that the time was ripe for the fall of the city because God had already humbled his own people, correcting the pride of the northern kingdom and then the southern. The Assyrians were spared so long, he says, only because God meant to use them for it.

Ellicott takes the opposite verb and builds much on it. He renders that the Lord restores the glory of Jacob so that it is as the glory of ancient Israel, though the plunderers marred their vine shoots, and resolves the construction by the two names: the first is the birth-name, the nation apart from its privileges, the homeless exile and younger son among nations, the second the name God gave the man who prevailed, so a people long called by the lesser name is to be known again by the greater. He rejects the alternative that the two names stand for the two kingdoms, the first having that force nowhere else. Clarke reports a bishop's emendation to the same effect but does not see that much is gained by it, keeping to the plain sense that the Lord had been opposed to Jacob and the enemy had prevailed. Keil and Delitzsch render with the turning away and pass on to the advancing army.
3:
Whose army is described is the first question, and the answers cross. Ellicott says the mighty men are the besieger's, and Gill agrees, taking them for the soldiers of Babylon and Media. Calvin records the reading that makes them Assyrians, meant to mark that people's shame, and dismisses it as too strained: the prophet describes the Chaldeans, armed so that their appearance alone would put their enemies to flight. Clarke goes the other way, referring the red shields and scarlet clothing to the preparations of the besieged.

Why the shields are red gets four explanations and a refusal. Ellicott says with blood, and rules out the bright red copper of which shields were made, since the word usually means dyed red; red, he adds, was the favourite colour of both nations in this siege. Gill offers three possibilities without choosing: the blood of the slain, a dye laid on to inject terror, or the glitter of gilded metal. Calvin reports a stranger account, that the shields were painted red so blood should not show and the soldiers clothed in red so they should not be frightened by their own wounds, which he says is recorded of an ancient people; but the habits of these nations being little known, he declines to decide.

The obscure word in the same verse divides them further. Ellicott renders that the chariots are equipped with flashing steel and inclines to take it of scythes fixed to the wheels, noting that one Greek writer credits a Persian king with inventing the scythed chariot while another makes it much older; the older Hebrew commentators rendered it torches. Calvin observes that the word occurs nowhere else, reports the Jewish view that its letters have been inverted and that it should be the word for torches used next, and concludes that lamps are meant, the chariots driving so impetuously that they seem flames of fire. Keil and Delitzsch keep the metal, rendering the chariots as in the fire of the steel-bosses.

The shaken trees are read as weapons by three, and Calvin gives an alternative he rejects. Clarke takes them for darts, arrows and javelins flung with destructive power, Ellicott that the cypress lances are brandished. Calvin reports that some translate the verb as stunned and apply it to the great men of Assyria, figured as trees and stupefied at the sight of their enemies; he prefers the lances, made of fir because the wood is light and flexible, so the picture is of shafts trembling in the soldiers' hands as trees toss in a forest. On the raging chariots of the next verse Gill takes them for the enemy's, driven furiously through the streets of the captured city, while reporting a Jewish reading that makes them the defenders' own, driving about like madmen because they dare not go out to fight; Clarke has both sets meeting there.

Ellicott restricts that verse to the besieged and rejects a modern reading of it. The contrast some have drawn, of order without and wild terror within, splendour without and a torchlight paleness within, he calls fanciful, refusing to make the last clause a description of the Ninevites' faces rather than their chariots. On the mustering that follows Gill again gives both possibilities, the invading kings recounting their officers or the Assyrian his own; Calvin sets out the same options, calls a proposed transposition too strained, and takes the verse of the Assyrians gathering every man of skill and courage, only to stumble in their marches like blind men through fear. Ellicott reaches the same picture and presses the last clause: it should read not that the defence is prepared but that the storming-shed has already been set against the wall, which the defenders ought to have prevented; and he quotes a modern authority on those engines, framed with osier, felt or skins, some fixed and some wheeled.
6:
The gates of the rivers are taken by Gill three ways: two named streams between which the city is said to have stood, the gates nearest the great river, or the river itself, which broke down two miles and a half of wall. Calvin makes the point rhetorical: that side was best defended, the current being famously rapid, and the prophet ridicules a confidence that thought enemies wholly shut out there, since God passes through rivers as easily as along a plain. The dissolving of the palace he takes with it, the fortresses melting of themselves as though the walls were paper and the stones water. Ellicott identifies the gates as the dams fencing the stream that ran through the city and the river outside, forced open by the swollen torrent.

Clarke and Ellicott rest the verse on the same ancient account and draw opposite conclusions. The story is that an oracle had said the city could not be taken till the river became an enemy to it; that in the third year of the siege continual rains swelled the water, flooded part of the city and threw down twenty stadia of wall; and that the king, taking the oracle fulfilled, burnt himself with his treasures and household in his palace, whereupon the besiegers entered by the breach. Clarke reads that as the literal fulfilment and takes the dissolving of the palace to mean that it was burnt. Ellicott holds the account inaccurate in detail but founded on fact, and takes the same verb literally, of a solid dissolved by water, against a modern commentator's figurative reading of it as the dissolution of the empire.

The word rendered as a name in the next verse is the hardest in the chapter, and produces five answers. Gill reports most of them: the Targum makes it the queen, Jewish commentators the queen's own name, others the king figured as a woman for the effeminacy historians record of the last of that line, others an idol, the palace, or the city. Clarke inclines to the queen, since the account of the burning names only the king, the concubines and the eunuchs, so she may be supposed to have escaped and been brought to the conqueror. Calvin calls the proper-name reading too strained, adopted only because something had to be said and no likelier conjecture offered, and refers the words to the state of the kingdom by personification; if a queen is meant, he would have it either that she was made manifest, the allusion being to the chambers where delicate women keep themselves, or that she was drawn into exile. Ellicott rejects the name outright, taking the form as a verb cognate with a word meaning of a certainty, so the sense is that it is decided; the laying bare is the figure of the virgin city shamed by capture, and the mourning maidens are probably her dependent towns. Keil and Delitzsch keep the name and render that she is led away captive.

Why the city is called a pool is answered historically by two and textually by two. Gill takes it for a place as full of people as a pool of fish, full also of unstable wealth and undisturbed from the beginning. Calvin makes the clause an answer to an objection, that antiquity lends kingdoms strength and authority, so a people who boasted they had always been, as another nation fabled its kingdom older than the world, could not believe there would be an end where there was no beginning. Clarke reports a bishop's rendering that the waters of the city are a pool of waters, referring it to the inundation, and Ellicott prefers a slight change of reading on the same lines, that her waters are like a pool and the inhabitants are fleeing, the streams that ran in courses and dykes being now one expanse of flood.
10:
The three words that open the passage are a sound-effect that will not carry over. Gill says only that the terms are heaped up to confirm the thing and that there is an elegant play here which English cannot express. Clarke shows what the play consists in: the words are of the same sound and grow longer as they go, so their very shape marks a desolation great, greater and greatest.

What happens to the faces divides Clarke from Ellicott. Clarke takes the blackness for a real change of complexion brought on by the famine, and supports it from a traveller's report that sickness so alters the countenance among certain Asiatic peoples that a man fair in health becomes nearly black. Ellicott prefers a withdrawal of brightness to a gathering of blackness, referring the reader to the same expression in an earlier prophet.

The lions are agreed to be the Assyrian kings. Gill names four of them and takes the figure of their strength, courage and cruelty. Clarke reads the den as the habitation of bold and ferocious men and the feeding place as the resort to which victorious generals returned; on the next verse he assigns each term its counterpart, the whelps being the sons and nobles, the lionesses the queen and concubines, the holes and dens the treasure-houses, palaces and wardrobes; and he calls the whole a very fine allegory admirably supported.

Henry presses the comparison until it turns against the men it describes. Cruel tyrants, he says, are worse than the beasts they are likened to, since being men humanity is expected of them and lions do not prey on their own kind; yet these walked in their city as a lion in the woods, feared by everybody and loved by nobody, which was all they desired. He then turns the tearing and strangling into a domestic excuse and refuses it: the king made it his business to enrich his own house, seizing what came near for his wives and children, and many defend their rapine by pleading that they have families to provide for, whereas what is got so never does them good. Gill leaves the text at that verse and reports an old opinion that the lioness bears but once in her life and then but one, refuted by a later writer out of two ancient authorities and disproved, he adds, by the prophet's own words.

At the last verse the speaker changes, and Calvin makes the change itself the point. Until now the prophet had been God's herald, giving the plunderers their commission; when God comes forward and declares his own decree without the mouth of a man, the effect is far more impressive. He notes the emphatic force of the demonstrative, God showing himself as though awakened from sleep to undertake his people's cause. Gill records the alternative rendering, that God will come to Nineveh rather than be against her, and adds that when the Lord of all armies is against a people nothing but ruin can follow.

The smoke in the same verse is read three ways. Calvin rejects the suggestion that it means no more than a smoky fire, and takes the sense to be that at the first onset the whole force of the city would be consumed, chariots standing for every kind of warlike preparation. Henry keeps the odd preposition and finds contempt in it: it is not said in the fire but in the smoke, so they are consumed while the fire of God's indignation does no more than smoke; or else the drivers are smothered where they sit. Keil and Delitzsch render the verse plainly, the chariots burned in smoke and the sword devouring the young lions. Clarke closes on the last clause, that the voice which announced splendid victories shall be heard no more, and the plunderer perish with his plunder.
